ABB Migration.notes:
# v8

Until now this tool decoded the project and stopped. Everything it wrote was
ABB's facts, tidied — correct, useful, and still in the source system's
vocabulary. That leaves both of its users one step short: the engineer migrating
to DeltaV had nothing DeltaV-shaped to work from, and the engineer who has never
used Freelance **could not see the logic at all** — `logic_connections.csv` is a
netlist, and `B-CT-713.3` means nothing without Freelance open next to it.

## Read the logic without Freelance

**The FBD sheets are now drawn.** Every coordinate was already in the export and
nothing was rendering them. `extracted_svg/logic/` holds one SVG per sheet plus a
contact sheet: blocks that carry a plant tag — the ones that become DeltaV
modules — are drawn heavier, wires and junctions are drawn exactly as the export
has them, signals entering and leaving the sheet are named, inverted pins get
their bubble, and hovering any block gives you its tag.

**`extracted_system/block_inventory.csv`** says what each block type *is*, in one
line, and — the useful part — whether it becomes a DeltaV module or folds into
somebody else's expression. `M_ANA` is an analog measurement and becomes an
`_AI_V01`; `AND` is logic and becomes a term inside a module, not a module of its
own. Getting that distinction wrong inflates a module count, and an estimate, by
an order of magnitude. Block types the legend does not cover are listed too,
ranked by instance count, so the gaps rank themselves — and adding one to
`freelance_refdata/block_library.json` needs no code change.

**Pin names** resolve where the export publishes them (the project's own function
blocks: `PUMP_FB.START`) and read as `#3` where it does not. The index convention
for standard-library blocks has never been confirmed against a real project, so a
bare number is never dressed up as a name; those pins are documented in the block
inventory instead.

## Restated for DeltaV

- **`proposed_modules.csv`** — what each tagged block should become: the PCSD
  `MODULE_CLASS`, the evidence, and the device parameters already recovered. Two
  independent signals are used — the ABB block class, and the type of IO channel
  the tag is wired to. When they agree the row is `confirmed`; when they disagree
  it is `conflict` and gets looked at rather than averaged; when neither fires it
  is a work item naming the block type to add, not a silent gap.
- **`controller_sizing.csv`** — per source controller: tags, modules, IO by type,
  cross-controller signals, fastest scan rate. The first-cut answer to how many
  DeltaV controllers this needs.
- **`peer_to_peer.csv`** — every signal used outside its owning controller, and
  what DeltaV needs in its place.
- **Scan rates are now legal.** DeltaV accepts a discrete set of module periods
  and 0.25 s is not one of them — a 250 ms Freelance task is the common case and
  would have failed on import. `deltav_scan_ms` snaps to the nearest accepted
  period, rounding **down**, so a loop never ends up running slower than the
  plant was tuned for.
- **`io_list.csv`** gained the target side: the DeltaV card / CHARM type per
  channel. Unrecognised modules are left blank — an IO list with a wrong card
  type is worse than one with a gap.

## Proving it is complete

- **`extracted_system/coverage.csv`** — every record type in the export and
  whether this tool decoded it. The parser used to end in *"all other tags fall
  through silently"*, which meant it could not tell you what it had missed;
  "lossless" was a claim rather than a measurement.
- **`alarm_list.csv`** — one row per configured alarm instead of sixteen columns
  per tag, so the alarm load can be counted and sorted by priority. Discrete
  alarms carry no limit and are included anyway; counting only limits
  under-reports the load by every discrete point in the plant.
- **`index.html` is now the report** — size of the job, shape per controller,
  what the logic is made of, and a *Needs a decision* sectio

SuperOPCWatchIt.notes:
# v6

**Fixed: listing the registered OPC servers crashed the helper on machines that
have classic OPC installed.**

The helper asked Windows for the OPC server-list object, then used the answer as
if it were a different kind of object and called through it — an access violation
that killed it silently, with no message to show. It only happened where classic
OPC (OPCEnum) is actually registered: everywhere else the request fails first and
the tool correctly reported "no classic OPC here", which is why this went unseen.
It now asks for the interface it intends to use, matching what the rest of the
helper already did.

Connecting to a server, browsing, reading and writing tags were unaffected.

DifFHX.notes:
# v11
- **The PDF no longer dies on its own bullet.** When the expected fonts were
  absent, report generation failed part-way through rather than falling back —
  so a comparison you had already waited for produced nothing.

## v11

- Fixed the replication map corrupting names it was never meant to touch. A rule of
  `_A` -> nothing, intended to map unit-A tags onto their unsuffixed counterparts, was
  a blind substring replace, so it also rewrote every other identifier containing `_A`:
  `USE_ALL_UNITS` became `USELL_UNITS`, `BAD_ACTIVE` became `BADCTIVE`, `HI_HI_ACT`
  became `HI_HICT`, `HC_AI` became `HCI` and `DTE_ALM_ACK` lost two pieces at once.
  On a real unit comparison that was 22 distinct corrupted values, and the report was
  mostly differences that were not differences.
- Replication rules now carry a **match mode**. Segment (the default) refuses to match
  against a neighbouring letter or digit; Suffix-only additionally refuses `_` and `-`,
  so a rule fires only at the end of a tag name. Anywhere (the old behaviour), Whole
  word, and full Regex with backreferences are also available per rule. Existing
  two-column maps keep working and pick up Segment mode, which is the fix.
- Added a **Preview** button to the map editor. It dry-runs the map over the parsed
  baseline and lists every value it would rewrite, grouped as distinct old -> new
  outcomes with hit counts, most frequent first, so an over-eager rule is one obvious
  line instead of something you discover by reading the finished report. Element names
  are covered too.
- Added **field scope**: library references are no longer translated at all, because the
  same string appears in every unit by design -- `MODULE_CLASS`, `SUB_TYPE`,
  `DEFINITION`, `CATEGORY` (Database Location), `DETAIL_DISPLAY`,
  `INSTRUMENT_AREA_DISPLAY`, `PRIMARY_CONTROL_DISPLAY`, `MMI_PICTURE`. They are still
  compared, just on the raw value, so a genuine class change is still reported. A custom
  template can override the list with `"no_translate_keys"`.
- Fixed replication rules cascading into each other. They were applied in sequence, so a
  map containing both `_A` -> `_B` and `_B` -> `_C` turned A-modules into C. All rules
  are now resolved in a single pass over the original text; where two could match at the
  same position the longer find wins.
- A `[Database Structure]` row caused by a translated child name now says what the name
  was matched as. These rows are the bulk of a bad map's output -- a mangled child name
  misses its counterpart, so the item is reported removed in one row and added in
  another -- and they were the only rows that gave no hint a rule had been involved.
- Added a **Regex Help** window covering the match modes, what each one does to a real
  `_A` rule, and ready-made patterns for FHX unit mapping.
- An invalid regex in the map no longer aborts the comparison: the offending rule is
  skipped, named in the run log, and flagged red in the editor.
- Internal: the comparison engine, the comparison template and the function-block
  reference maps now live in `shared/fhxdiff/` instead of being duplicated here and in
  FHXMerge. The two tools carried byte-identical forks of all three files, which is how
  the replication-map bug above existed in two tools at once and was nearly fixed in only
  one. `CompareParsedFHXs.py`, `TemplateManager.py` and `FB_Refs.py` remain as thin shims,
  so every call site is unchanged; both tools' test suites assert they resolve to the
  shared copy, so re-forking fails a test rather than drifting quietly.

FHXport.notes:
## v27

Module Report — from user feedback that modules known to exist were missing.

- **Unit modules are no longer missing.** The Module Report only ever listed
  control and equipment modules; unit modules were absent entirely. They are
  stored differently in the FHX — the name and class sit on the outer block and
  everything else on a nested child — so a scan of the top level of each block
  found nothing on them. Measured on two real exports: **35** and **66** unit
  modules recovered that had never appeared.
- **The report is now an Excel workbook** with a sheet each for Modules and Unit
  Modules, instead of one flat CSV. Note the output file is now
  `<name>_ModuleReport.xlsx` — if you have a script picking up the `.csv` by
  name, it needs updating. Both sheets carry the same columns, are sorted by tag,
  and open with a bold header row and columns sized to their contents.
- **Inherited values are no longer blank.** A module that does not set its own
  description, primary display, period or controller now shows the one it takes
  from its module class, which is what DeltaV itself shows. Every other cell is
  byte-for-byte what the old report produced.
- **New columns on both sheets.** `MODULE_TYPE` and `MODULE_SUBTYPE` — populated
  on 3,167 of 3,242 modules on a real export, and absent from this report
  entirely until now — plus `INSTRUMENT_AREA_DISPLAY` and `DETAIL_DISPLAY`, which
  complete the set of displays a module names alongside the primary control
  display. They are spelled as the Historian Report spells them, so the two
  reports line up side by side.
- **New columns on the Unit Modules sheet**, for the batch settings a unit module
  has and a control module does not: `MAX_OWNERS` (how many batches may own the
  unit at once), `SIMULATED`, `DOWNSTREAM_UNITS_OPTION`, and counts of the
  `PHASE_COUNT` and `ALIAS_COUNT` the unit carries — the phase count separates a
  real batch unit from a bare equipment grouping at a glance.
- **Column order changed.** Description, type and subtype now lead, and the three
  displays sit together at the end.

Three attributes every unit module carries are deliberately left out.
`MMI_PICTURE` is byte-identical to `PRIMARY_CONTROL_DISPLAY` on every unit module
in both reference exports, so it would ship the same fact twice; `ID` is an
internal DeltaV record number, not configuration; and the `UNIT` child block is
empty.

The Unit Modules sheet names its class column `UNIT_CLASS`, since a unit module's
class is a unit module class and not a lookup into the module class library.

## v26

Reference Report — it no longer dies on large exports, and it is roughly 50x faster.

- **It stops running out of memory.** The report used to copy the whole element
  tree two or three times over and then copy every module class into every one of
  its instances, so peak memory was several times the size of the export. On a big
  plant export that exhausted the machine, and the tool vanished with no error at
  all — the failure happened below Python, so there was nothing to report. It now
  reads the definitions in place instead of copying them. Measured on three real
  exports: **578 MB → 2 MB**, **897 MB → 2 MB**, **1017 MB → 0.4 MB**.
- **And it is far faster** — the same three exports went from **115s, 135s and 91s
  to 2.3s, 2.2s and 3.2s**. Every row is byte-for-byte what the old version
  produced.
- **A report bigger than a worksheet no longer fails.** Excel holds 1,048,576 rows
  per sheet, and the Unknown References tab can exceed that on a whole-plant
  export; the write used to fail at the very end, after all the work. Overflow now
  continues onto `Unknown References (2)`.
- **Expression text can no longer abort the write.** Control characters copied out
  of raw FHX are rejected by Excel; they are now stripped, and over-long values
  trimmed to what a cell can hold. This applies to every report the tool writes.
- **Aliased references now show their node.** The Referenced Node

FHXEdit.notes:
## v10

- **A regex helper.** Ticking "Regex" in Advanced Find and Replace now opens a helper
  panel. Build a pattern from plain text -- type the literal you are looking for, pick
  contains / starts with / ends with / equals, and it escapes the special characters
  for you, so a value like AI1$PV becomes a pattern that actually matches it. Buttons
  insert the common pieces (digits, a number, any text, a word, space, start, end, a
  group, or) at the cursor.
- **Test a pattern before you run it.** Type a sample value, or pull one straight out
  of your search results, and the helper shows live whether the pattern matches and
  exactly what the replacement would produce -- computed by the same code the Replace
  buttons use, so the preview cannot disagree with the result.
- **Capture groups are shown, not guessed.** Each ( ) group is listed with what it
  captured and a button to drop \1, \2 into Replace. A group that swallowed a "/" or a
  space is flagged, which almost always means a .* is matching more than intended.
- The helper also warns about a pattern with leading or trailing spaces (with one-click
  Trim), about greedy .* and .+, and about writing \12 in the replacement -- Python
  reads that as capture group 12, not group 1 followed by "2".
- **Scripted Edits (Ctrl+R)** -- a new window for the transforms find-and-replace
  cannot express: comparing numbers, building one field from another, adding or
  removing a field, and renaming from a mapping table. Ready-made examples cover
  inventory counts, a field inspector, a CSV dump, a numeric clamp, a cross-field
  description builder, a mapping-table rename and structural add/remove; a reference
  panel lists the whole API.
- **Running a script changes nothing.** It collects the edits it would make and lists
  every one -- location, field, before, after -- and the file is untouched until you
  press Apply. Applying is a single undo step: undo reverses the whole script,
  including added and removed fields, putting each one back in its original position
  in the file.
- Scripts run in the background with a Cancel button, and a loop that never ends is
  stopped automatically instead of freezing the window.
- Fields are written through an API that keeps a value, its quoting and its position
  in the file consistent. Editing the tree directly could silently drop a newly added
  field when the file was exported; this cannot.

## v9

- Advanced Find and Replace can now match with regular expressions. Tick the new
  "Regex" box and every text field on the dialog -- Find, Target Key Contains, and the
  Classifier and Name boxes on the target row and on every ancestor layer -- is read as
  a pattern instead of as literal text. Previously all five were plain "contains"
  tests, so there was no way to express alternatives, anchors, or digit runs.
- "Exact Match Only" now means "anchor the pattern to the whole value" when Regex is
  on, so `^(HI|LO)_LIM$` in Target Key selects those two keys and nothing else, and
  `^AI$` as a Classifier no longer drags in AI_ALARM.
- Groups captured in Find expand in Replace as \1, \2, and so on. Finding
  `^FIC_(\d+)$` and replacing with `FC-\1` renumbers an entire naming convention in
  one pass.
- A pattern that will not compile is reported against the box it came from and the
  search is abandoned, rather than half-running. Replacements resolve every new value
  before any of them are applied, so a bad pattern -- or a \9 that names no captured
  group -- cannot leave some rows rewritten and others not. Undo still records the
  whole replacement as one step.
- Note that with Regex ticked, characters such as . $ and ( become pattern syntax, so
  an FHX value like AI1$PV has to be written AI1\$PV. With Regex off, matching is
  literal exactly as before.

EMTools.notes:
# v5
Generate now works against every PCSD template, not just the command-driven one, and
performs the device fix-up that previously had to be done by hand in DeltaV.

Device references now follow the rename:
- Renaming a device slot (`DEV1` → your alias) now reaches the composites, not just
  the block declarations. MONITOR's failure roll-up, the command SFC confirm
  expressions and the ACQ_REL acquire/release statements all addressed `/DEV1/`
  directly and were left pointing at blocks that no longer existed — every generated
  EM shipped with dead device monitoring and step confirmations, at every device
  count, on every template type.
- Requesting fewer devices than a template ships now removes the surplus slots
  properly: per-device elements are deleted, structured-text statements dropped, and
  boolean clauses pruned with their connector so the expression stays balanced. A
  prune that would unbalance an expression is refused and reported instead.
- Multi-slot comment boxes (the arbitration instructions, the template changelog) are
  left alone on purpose; single-slot `(DEV1 : SHARED)` labels are rewritten.

Command slots are cleaned up the same way:
- Unused command blocks were deleted but still referenced — the HOLD composite
  disabled all ten, each command's SFC re-enabled them, and MONITOR tested every one.
  Generating a 2-command EM left 112 references to blocks that were not in the file.
- The MONITOR function block pointed at the template's original composite name after
  that composite had been renamed, so it referenced a definition not present in the
  output. Now renamed together, as COMMAND and ACQ_REL already were.

- The SFC branches for unused command slots are now cut out of the logic rather than
  left testing the stock library set. A 2-command CMD EM's HOLD sequence goes from 12
  steps and 22 transitions to 4 and 6. A branch is only removed when every route into
  it is dead, so nothing reachable is ever dropped, and conditionals the pruning
  empties are collapsed with it.
- No reference to a stock named set survives anywhere in a generated EM.

Found by importing generated EMs into a real DeltaV 15.0 — all three parsed and
round-tripped cleanly and still failed to import:
- Composite names over DeltaV's 16-character limit were silently abbreviated while
  the EM kept referencing the full name, so the module class would not import at all.
  Names are now built inside the limit and de-duplicated.
- The generated named set was written after the composites that use it, so every
  expression logged "unresolved enumeration reference". It is now emitted first.
- Pruning a trimmed device from a flat boolean chain took the statement terminator
  with it, leaving a dangling `AND` and a syntax error. A prune that would leave an
  expression malformed is now refused rather than shipped.

Two additions that make the tool say what it did and what it needs:
- **The Commands list now shows the composite each command will produce.** DeltaV caps
  item names at 16 characters, so "Transfer" on a long EM name becomes
  `TRANSFER_TST_CMD`. The generator shortens names itself now (it has to), and the
  summary line calls out which ones were shortened along with the resulting class and
  named-set names.
- **Overview ▸ Dependencies…** lists what the target database must already contain —
  composites, device classes and named sets — before you attempt an import. DeltaV
  only reports these one failure at a time, and each one cascades into whatever
  referenced it, so the real cause is usually well above the reported error. Works on
  imported documents as well as generated drafts.

Parameter CSV import fixed — it depended on the file's byte count:
- Loading tried UTF-16-LE first and fell back on `UnicodeDecodeError`, but UTF-16-LE
  decodes *any* even-length byte sequence without raising. A UTF-8 CSV whose byte
  count happened to be even decoded into mojibake, matched no columns, and imported
  **nothing at all** — si

## v4

- Merge any number of FHX files, not just two. The setup screen now takes a list of
  files (browse or drag and drop) whose order sets precedence, and the decision panel
  shows one diff pane and one "Keep" button per file.
- Fixed the decision buttons appearing to do nothing. A decision on an element that was
  identical in both files was recorded but the row kept reporting "Auto-Merged", so
  Keep A / Keep B / Discard all looked dead — including Discard, which silently dropped
  the element from the export. Rows now always show the decision that is in force, the
  selection highlight no longer paints over the row's colour, and every decision is
  echoed in a new status bar.
- Clicking a decision button with nothing selected, or with a category row selected,
  now says so instead of failing silently.
- A file that does not contain the selected element can no longer be picked for it: that
  file's button is disabled and its pane is marked "missing". Batch decisions skip those
  elements and report how many were skipped.
- Export no longer dead-ends on unresolved elements — it offers to fill them from the
  first file that contains each one — and reports how many elements came from each file.
- Added: keyboard shortcuts (Alt+1..9 to keep a file's version, Alt+D to discard),
  multi-select decisions, "jump to next conflict after a decision", per-category pending
  counts, and "fill every remaining conflict from <file>".
- Large files open immediately: element children are now built when a row is expanded
  instead of expanding the entire file up front.

- Fixed very large FHX files appearing to hang while loading. The step that learns how
  to name elements uniquely searched every combination of up to five attributes, which
  on a wide export ran to hundreds of millions of attempts and never completed. Files

Logix2dv.notes:
# v6

**Bulk Edit CSV + FMT can be exported from the window.** One tab-separated pair
per matched PCSD class, every device of that class a row with the parameters
recovered from the source filled in. It had been reachable only from the command
line, which meant the output meant for the engineer doing the migration was the
one output they could not produce.

**The narrative is written for someone who works in DeltaV.** It is the spec for
the logic no class covers, so it is read by people who may never have opened
Studio 5000 — and it was handing them Rockwell comment syntax:
`(* P_ValveC(FCV306004) when (Simulate) -- manual *)`. That now reads *"WHEN
(Simulate) THEN FCV306004 is a valve (device control) module (Rockwell P_ValveC)
— configure it as one in DeltaV"*, and an instruction with no DeltaV block says
so in words instead of leaving a marker.

**Two valves on one card are two devices, not one device called "Local".** The
cross-reference collapses `Local:12:O.Ch3Data` to `Local`, so a section grouped
its rungs under the rack they shared rather than under `FCV306004` and
`FCV306005`. A device is named from the instrument the rung instantiates, and an
I/O card is never the subject or a listed signal source. The channels get their
own line instead — *Field I/O: Local:4:I.Ch13Data (AI), Local:12:O.Ch3Data (AO)*
— because each one becomes a DST.

**Valves and motors now wire their I/O.** A composite discrete device has no nested
channel block; its I/O goes into a bank of reference slots (`IO_OUT_1..4` for the
commands, `INPUT_D1..4` for the feedbacks, or the bare `INPUT`/`OUTPUT` assemblies
on a networked drive), and every slot is declared as an internal connection. The
binder only ever looked at input/output-connection ports, so on `MCP_CUP.L5X` all
24 valves fit their class and wired nothing at all. Points now go into the bank
that matches their direction. A control loop likewise binds *both* its channel
blocks — only the first was bound, which left every loop's output channel unwired.
An I/O point the class has nowhere to reference (a modulating valve's position
feedback, which DeltaV resolves inside the device block) is reported rather than
dropped.

**Unwired ports meant three different things and were reported as one.** The banks
are fixed-size: a valve with one solenoid uses `IO_OUT_1` and leaves three spare,
and those three were listed as missing wiring — 96 of the project's 143 "unbound
ports" were empty slots on valves, telling the engineer to wire channels that do
not exist. A bank now counts once, and only when nothing in it landed. Separately,
a class's optional capabilities — a loop's cascade input, feedforward, and
pressure/temperature compensation — are what the class *offers*, not what the
conversion *owes*: a loop with no cascade source is not a loop with missing
wiring, so those are listed as unused class capabilities instead.

**Two numbers, because there are two questions.** The match percentage says whether
the class is the right one. It took four distinct values across 280 modules,
because it reported which scoring rule fired — so a device with its channel, its
engineering range and its alarm limits scored exactly the same as one with only a
channel. Alongside it there is now a completeness percentage: what was actually
recovered, listed item by item, and what was not.

**A tie between `_AI_V01` and `_AI_CR_V01` is not a decision anyone can make.**
Ladder logic cannot distinguish the AI variants and never will, so "ambiguous —
confirm the correct class variant" was 24 punch-list items nobody could act on.
A tie *within* a device kind now reads as the variant being undetermined with the
plainest taken, and stays off the work list; a tie *across* kinds — a valve
scoring level with a motor, where the wrong device ships silently — is flagged as
the only one worth anyone's time. (The tie test also never fired on the commonest
real case: 0.93 minus 0.88 is 0.05000000000000004 in binary, so `<= 0.05` said no.)

  now appears complete, with its element, thermowell, transmitter, controller and
  control valve together.

  on these drawings, and because the grid is read from the margins outside that

  readings worth a second look. Deliberately a report, not an auto-correct: tags are

# v6
- **32-bit binaries load at the right image base**, so addresses in the report
  line up with the file being examined.
- **Reads an undocumented MFC file format** by working it out from the binary

# v6 (not yet built)
**`patina carchive` — read an undocumented MFC file format out of the binary
that writes it.** Aimed at the case where the binary is not the artefact you
care about: a proprietary document format with no schema.

- **The `CRuntimeClass` table** with each class's `sizeof`, its **archive
  schema**, and its base. The schema is the fact that matters and Patina was
  discarding it: a class whose schema is `0xFFFF` is `DECLARE_DYNAMIC`, so
  `CArchive` **never announces it by name** — a reader that expects every class
  to be tagged will mis-frame every record after the first.
- **The inlined `CArchive` fixed-width accessors**, with each one's **field
  width** and direction. Direction is decided by which side of the `mov` the
  archive buffer is on, not by anything sitting near it.

Validated against an independently hand-derived model of `GraphicsEd.dll`
(FactoryTalk View's graphics editor): 360 classes, and every checkable fact
agrees — `ZText` 504 bytes deriving from `ZUnrotatedRect`, `ZButtonElement` 3480
deriving from `ZPolygon`, the three `ZConnection*` classes alone at schema 1,
`ZDrawingElement`/`ZUnrotatedRect` both `DECLARE_DYNAMIC` and sharing one
`Serialize` at `0x6244ff90`. Generalises: RSLinx gives 198 classes and 4
primitives; a non-MFC binary reports nothing.

- **`patina rtti` reported `[0 method(s)]` for every vtable in a 32-bit binary**

  stride. 1,980 of 1,980 wrong on one DLL, now 0.
- **Base-class recovery missed every shared-MFC (`_AFXDLL`) binary.** The getter

  frame and behind a two-hop thunk. `carchive` decodes instead of byte-matching;

The quality column was inverted — every good sample was flagged bad

what is actually not-good, and the read summary says how many samples were not
good. The CSV export gains `quality`, `substatus`, `limit` and `is_good` columns
alongside the raw bytes, which are unchanged.

# v12

- **A find/replace no longer changes anything you did not ask it to.** Two defects
  fired on every FHX FnR wrote, with no rules involved at all — a read-then-save
  round trip was enough to reproduce both.
  - The UTF-16 byte-order mark was dropped. The reader stripped it and the writer
    never put it back, so every output was BOM-less UTF-16 — which is what DeltaV's
    FHX import reads as ANSI. Whether the source had one is now remembered and
    reproduced, rather than guessed at either way.
  - Line endings were rewritten. Both ends used default newline translation, so a
    lone CR came back as CRLF. Measured on the corpus: 8 of them, inside a `rem`
    block in an expression, adding 8 lines to every replicated file. Read and write
    are now byte-faithful, and a no-op round trip is byte-identical — pinned by a
    test, on a 3.6 MB real export as well as a fixture.

- **Composite named-set references are renamed on both sides.** `'_SET:VALUE'` was
  taken as one candidate. Both halves carry the unit suffix, a suffix transform
  rewrites only the trailing one, and because the composite is the longest find in
  the map it wins the span — so the correct rule for the set name, sitting right
  beside it, could never fire. The result was an expression referring to a named set
  that does not exist in the replicate: measured at 33 occurrences per file, in all
  five replicates. The reference is now split at the colon and each half gets its
  own rule.

  The general check matters more than the instance: no derived rule may leave the
  thing that identifies the source unit in its replacement. Any that does is flagged
  in the preview as a HALF-DONE RENAME rather than quietly applied, because a rule
  like that is worse than a missing one — it fires, consumes the text, and blocks
  the rule that would have finished the job.

- **Class bindings are found, and left as a decision.** `CLASS="..."` attributes and
  `BATCH_EQUIPMENT_UNIT_MODULE_CLASS` declarations were read by nothing, so
  `MAKEUP_BA`/`SURGE_BA` survived into all five replicates and every one of them
  bound to the original's class. They are now listed under "Not included" with the
  reason, and renamed only if you say so — a shared class across replicates is a
  legitimate design, and the tool should not decide that for you.

- **A written FHX is now checked for what the rename missed.** The graphics pass
  already re-read every file it wrote and listed references still holding an old
  value; the text pass had no equivalent, and its only check was structural. A file
  with 33 dangling references parses perfectly. Any find term still present in the
  saved file is now reported with a count, in the log, next to the success line.

- **The graphics engine is rebuilt and re-vendored, and it fixes a defect that
  damaged files.** A find/replace whose replacement is *longer* than what it
  replaced took the grow path, which shifts every heap offset — and nothing
  relocated the pointers to the DeltaV dynamo substitution parameters. Measured on
  one picture: 31 parameters in, 11 out, all garbage, with validation reporting
  0 errors throughout. Same-length and shortening rules were always safe, which is
  why a `_BA` → `_A` replication never saw it. Confirmed fixed in iFIX.

  **If you rewrote graphics with an earlier build using a rule that made a name
  LONGER, check them.** Those pictures load, and their faceplate calls, data
  sources and navigation links may be dead. `bstrscan --damaged <folder>` in
  OperateTools finds them without opening anything (0 false positives over 1,315
  stock Emerson pictures). A damaged picture has to be regenerated — the loss is
  detectable but not reversible.

- **VBA source can be rewritten too.** `fr --vba` existed only in the GUI binary's
  argument parser, so the CLI FnR drives could not reach it and a tag hardcoded in a
  picture's script survived every rename. Added to `operate-cli` and surfaced as a
  "Rewrite VBA sour

CornerRDP.notes:
# v8

- **The remote screen keeps up now.** Every action against a node — a click, a keystroke,
  a refresh — used to sit for about six and a half seconds before the screen came back,
  and on a desktop with anything moving on it (a blinking cursor, a clock, a console
  scrolling) it could stall for the better part of a minute. That was not the network and
  not the node: the engine decided the screen had "stopped changing" by waiting three full
  seconds for silence, twice per action, whether or not anything was still happening. It
  now samples the connection twenty times a second and moves on as soon as the picture has
  genuinely settled. **Measured against a live station: 6.6 seconds down to about 0.2.**
- **Screens travel lighter.** A full 1280x1024 screen went from 221 KB to 119 KB — a 46%
  cut — by dropping a byte per pixel that a remote desktop never uses and compressing the
  rest properly. Same picture, no quality lost, noticeably quicker over a slow link.

# v6

- **Reaches stations it simply could not before.** Four faults in the connection engine each
  made a whole class of node unreachable, and each looked like "this machine is too old to talk
  to". None of them were. Nothing has to be changed on a node for any of this.
  - A station that only allows the **legacy Remote Desktop security layer** was handed a
    scrambled encryption key, so it saw nonsense and hung up without a word.
  - A station that requires an **older TLS version** than the engine offered was refused
    outright. The engine now falls back to Windows' own TLS, which still speaks it — enabled for
    that one connection, nothing changed on your PC.
  - An older station that **packs several screen updates into one message** had all but the
    first thrown away, and the connection died on the first refresh.
  - A screen update **larger than the area it was meant to fill** crashed the decoder outright.
- **Measured on a 47-node lab fleet: 44 now connect, up from 41**, and every remaining failure
  is a rejected password rather than anything about the protocol.

# v5

- **Push, Pull and Deploy agent now work on nodes that refuse admin file sharing.** They were
  wired straight to `\\host\C$`, so on a hardened station — most of a real DeltaV fleet — they
  simply failed, even though the Screen tab could drive that same node perfectly. They now take
  whichever door the node opens: admin file sharing, WinRM, or, when the Screen tab has a live
  session, the Remote Desktop session itself.
- **A node you can see is now a node you can copy files to.** The last route needs nothing
  installed on the target at all: the file rides the Remote Desktop connection and the node is
  asked to hash what it received, so a transfer either verifies or fails — it never half-lands
  quietly.
- **The status line now says which route carried the work**, rather than leaving you to guess
  why something that worked on one station fails on the next.

DVEmu.notes:
# v6

Runs a configuration the way the controller does in more places, and will now run one
without a window at all.

- **A command line.** `DVEmu.exe --coverage plant.fhx`, `--scenario fill.json`, `--sweep
  cases.json`, `--list-areas`, `--list-controllers`, and `--report out.html|csv|xml` —
  so a configuration can be checked from a script or a build instead of by hand. No
  display needed; the window still opens when you pass no options. `--help` used to
  print nothing at all, because the tool ships windowed and a windowed process has no
  console. It borrows the calling terminal's now.

  One Windows wart worth knowing: PowerShell's `>` does not give a windowed program a
  place to write, so `DVEmu.exe --coverage > out.txt` writes an empty file *in
  PowerShell*. Pipe instead — `DVEmu.exe --coverage plant.fhx | Out-File out.txt` — or
  redirect from `cmd`, both of which capture everything. `--report FILE` is unaffected:
  the tool writes that file itself.

- **Flow metering (AGA_US / AGA_SI) is modelled.** Meter-type dispatch, the orifice and
  turbine paths, the AGA3 limits of use, every documented `ERROR_STATE` with the status
  it contributes, and the whole totalisation contract — `TIMER_ACCUM` roll-over to the
  `LAST_` parameters, `RESET_ACCUM`, flowing hours, and the `PCT_` companions. Two
  published equation sets (the AGA8 detail method and the ISO6976 heating value) are not
  reproduced, and the coverage report says so rather than quietly returning a number.

- **Coverage says what it does not model.** A block that runs but passes part of its
  answer through now declares it, and `--coverage` prints those limits with an instance
  count. The distinction between "we compute this" and "we pass this through" was
  previously invisible.

- **Statuses read and drive correctly.** `X.ST` reads a parameter's status byte, so the
  many guards written as `'X.ST' = 128` or `>= 64` decide instead of staying unknown —
  but a configuration that defines a real parameter of that name (456 of them in one
  plant) keeps it. Driving a status now actually drives it, which is what replay needs.

- **Array parameters download.** Indexed defaults such as a gas composition were stored
  under a name nothing could read, so blocks that depend on one started empty.

- **More of the language.** All 37 documented expression functions, checked against the
  worked examples in the documentation; `WHILE` loops, array elements and `VAR`
  declarations; `REM` comments. An unimplemented call is now recorded and reported
  instead of silently evaluating to unknown.

- **More blocks.** `DTE` (Date Time Event), `RS`/`SR` flip-flops, `RET`, `ISEL`, `INT`,
  `MLTX`, `SPLTR`, `FLTR`, fieldbus `FFAI`/`FFAO`, and the state-driven PCSD equipment
  module. A device block now picks its setpoint input by mode, as the real one does.

## v7

**Runs on Windows Server 2016 and Windows 10 1607.**

On those builds the window never opened — the tool stopped with "DLL load failed
while importing QtGui: The specified module could not be found." and nothing else.

# v1

First release. Consolidates **FMTMaker**, **FMTExport** and **ModExport** into one
tool; all three are retired by this release.

## If you used the old tools, read this

Three of the fixes below change the output you will get. They are all corrections,
but they are not silent.

- **FMTExport read the wrong columns from most real templates.** It took the
  parameter line to be the line after `header`, but `must_exist` sits between the
  two — so on 49 of the 62 Emerson PCSD templates it used the literal text
  `must_exist area` as its column list. If you built a workflow around that
  output, FMTTools will give you different (correct) columns.
- **The `.fmt` and its data file disagreed.** The spec declared a tab separator
  while the data was written as comma-separated CSV, so the pair could not import.
  FMTTools writes the data with whatever separator the `.fmt` declares. A
  comma-separated copy is still available as an explicit "for Excel" option.
- **ModExport exported one module, not one per class.** A `return` inside its
  element loop stopped it at the first module with a plant area.

## New

- All nine FMT directives are read and written — `object_subtype`, `must_exist`
  and `skip_lines` were never emitted before, and the object type was hardcoded to
  `Module`.
- **55 object types**, with their exact `begin_format_defn` tokens taken from
  DeltaV's own export engine — up from the 12 the shipped templates cover.
  `EIOC`, `SIS_Module`, `Logic_Solver`, `Modbus_Port`, `WIOC`, `Process_Cell`,
  `Recipe_Parameter`, `Hart_Device`, `Control_Tag`, `PHYSICAL_DEVICE`,
  `LOGICAL_DEVICE`, `SIGNAL` and the rest are all selectable. Each says whether
  its columns come from a shipped template or from documentation.
- **29 documented column contracts** (365 fields with valid values and
  required-for-import flags) from DeltaV's *Valid field values* tables. Enough to
  produce a correct starter worksheet and a valid specification for an object
  type no shipped template covers — OPC UA, Modbus TCP, EtherNet/IP, IEC 61850
  devices and signals, SIS modules, logic solvers, EIOCs.
- The 62 Emerson PCSD format specifications ship with the tool, usable as
  starting points.
- An **I/O** tab, both directions. Pick an object type, get a starter worksheet
  with exactly the columns it needs, fill it in, and get back the `.fmt` + data
  pair — column matching ignores order, case and padding, and anything that does
  not line up either way is reported rather than dropped silently. Or go the
  other way and read the I/O already in an FHX export (`Card`, `Channel`,
  `Charm_IO`). Large exports are streamed: a 274 MB system export is read
  without loading it whole.
- A **Validate** tab: check a `.fmt` and its data file before importing.
- A headless CLI: `FMTTools.exe cli --help` — including `sheet` and `pair` for the
  I/O round trip.

## Fixed

- `is_a_string_parameter` is derived rather than guessed. The old rule matched
  column names against seven substrings and was 87.4% correct against Emerson's
  own templates; specs built from a real export now agree on every shared column.
- Alarm suppression timeouts: the formatter failed outright on any value that was
  not angle-wrapped, and mis-carried the minutes above 1440 (1500 minutes came out
  as `1:1:1440` rather than `1:1:0`).
- Spare DCC conditions were emitted with an index of 0, which does not exist.

- Array-indexed parameters are kept on module instances; ModExport dropped them.
- A Library export now explains that its modules are templates with no plant area,

# InstrumentLab — release notes

## v3 — a new icon (2026-08-07)

**The icon now looks like an application and names the right trade.** It was line
art on a transparent background, while every other tool in the suite wears a bold
graphic on a filled tile — so on a shelf beside them it read as a fragment of a
drawing rather than as software. It was also only ever checked at large size, and
the idea it was built around, an unfilled wet leg, disappeared entirely by the size
it actually gets shown at.

It is now a vessel with a level in it and the instrument measuring it, and it is
drawn twice: a detailed version for large sizes and a simpler, bolder one for the
small sizes, so it stays readable in the taskbar rather than turning to mush.

Nothing else changed in this release.

## v2 — the butterfly valve gets its bore back (2026-08-07)

**A butterfly valve is a ring, and this one was a solid puck.** Its body was drawn
as a filled cylinder, and the bore, the liner and the disc all belong to the
cutaway — so in the as-installed view the solid outer wall was the entire picture.
It read, accurately, as "just a fat disc". The body is now a proper annular ring
you can see through, with the boss that carries the gearbox mounting pad, because
a wafer body is not a bare hoop.

Built as four surfaces rather than revolved from a profile: revolving smooths the
shading along the profile and rounds every corner off, which turned an eight-inch
cast body into something closer to a tyre. Separate surfaces keep the corners hard
while the bore stays round.

**Two parts were being drawn sealed shut.** The helper that makes a cylinder
quietly ignored the flag that opens its ends, so anything asking for a tube got a
capped one. The butterfly's liner and the vortex meter's shedder cage were both
built that way.

Nothing else changed: 31 figures, 0 failing, 0 floating parts, 943 tests.

## v1 — first release, and the first tool in Training (2026-08-06)

**Learn a process instrument by running it.** Thirty-one measuring technologies
across level, flow, temperature, pressure, analytical, valves and pumps — every one
simulated rather than described. Pick a variable, pick a technology, and optionally
a specific model; a model appears only once its datasheet has been read and its
numbers checked, so an empty shelf means "not verified yet" rather than "nothing
here".

**Three ways to work on each one.** *Overview* gives the measuring principle, an
annotated section, and the governing equations typeset with every symbol defined —
and a card that carries your own workbench values into the arithmetic, so the maths
is for the install you just built. *Workbench* is free play with no quiz: set the
process, the installation, the device and the faults, and watch the measurement
respond against an error budget. *3-D* shows the instrument as installed and in
cutaway, with the internals moving.

dead leg or an orifice plate fitted backwards cannot be seen from outside the pipe.
Those are figures rather than a scene you fly around, deliberately — a view you can

# v6
It asks DeltaV what is waiting, instead of guessing

Scanning the network used to say nothing at all about decommissioned nodes.
That was not a subtle failure: the probe built its list of addresses from the
device table, and a node with no identity is at none of them, so it swept
twenty-two addresses the node could not be at and never looked at the one place
it was. The single question most people open this tool to ask went unanswered.

**It now reads the list out of DeltaV itself.** DeltaV keeps Decommissioned
Nodes inside its comm layer, and the function that returns it turns out to be
one DvScan can call - the same one DeltaV Diagnostics uses to draw that view.
So the answer is exact rather than inferred: a row per node, with no packet
capture and no Administrator. On the system this was built against it returned
twenty-two nodes, including two that had spent two days refusing to appear
anywhere else.

Where that call is unavailable it falls back to probing the default address,
and is careful about what that proves. Every unassigned node answers on the
same address, so a probe can say **at least one** node is waiting and cannot
say how many. It says "at least one" rather than inventing a count.

**A CIOC or WIOC now says why it cannot be released, instead of offering.** A
CHARM or wireless I/O card keeps its commissioning in the I/O Port's
non-volatile memory, and the ProfessionalPLUS is not used to commission one at
all - so decommissioning in Explorer, removing a binding, and anything DvScan
can send are all aimed at the wrong place. It comes up decommissioned only on a
PHYSICAL change: move the card to another slot, or for a redundant pair, swap
the two. A virtual card has to be rebuilt, which is Emerson's own workaround in
KBA NK-1600-0143. The tool now explains all of that in place rather than
presenting a button that quietly does nothing.

**And a redundant node cannot be released one card at a time.** A redundant
CIOC node is one node made of two cards and the identity belongs to the pair,
so powering off the active card just hands it to the partner. That is now said
out loud.

**A fault in v5, fixed.** Building the release frame for a node with no binding
on disk substituted only the target address and left the rest of a real
captured frame in place - so it broadcast a decommission naming a controller
from another system entirely. It refuses to build a frame it cannot build
honestly, and the confirmation now decodes and shows the identity it is about
to send rather than only its size.

**Cards are recognised by what the device table calls them.** The old test knew
one naming convention and failed on any other, so on a system whose cards are
named CIOC-1 and CIOC-2 every card was audited as an ordinary node.

Also: the download manifest is no longer misread as though it carried a header
it has never had, and each finding now distinguishes which kind of network
evidence stands behind it.

# v5
A real decommission was captured, and it is a message we can send

DeltaV was recorded taking a controller out of service — the one event this
tool has never seen from either side, and the exact mirror of the failure it
exists for. An orphaned controller is one whose teardown never happened, and
until now nobody here had watched a teardown happen.

**The teardown is the identity push with the device id set to zero.** Same
class 0x0A message, same target MAC, same assigned addresses, same controller
name — only the device id differs. Eight copies go out inside a millisecond,
four from each control network, broadcast rather than addressed to the node.
Four captures of the same controller settle it beyond argument: the
re-commission and the cold-boot re-push both carry a real device id, and a
decommissioned controller idling at its default address draws none at all.

**Which means an orphan can be recovered.** The message DeltaV uses to
decommission is broadcast and selected by MAC, with no send-side gate — so it
reaches a con

# SuperDocs — release notes

## v1

First release.

**Reads compiled help without the product.** A clean-room ITSF/LZX reader
(`shared/chm`) decodes `.chm` from the on-disk format — no `hh.exe`, no install,
no third-party decompressor. Validated against DeltaV Books Online: 116 of 116
books decode with every entry byte-exact.

**One library, one search.** `.chm`, PDF and exported-HTML folders ingest into a
single SQLite store with an FTS5 index. The 116 DeltaV books become 16,811
topics and 3.1 M words in a 190 MB file — 67 MB less than the content it holds,
because 2,612 topics are byte-identical across books and are stored once. Search
across the whole library returns in under 3 ms.

**Search that takes what you type.** Quoted phrases, `-exclusions`, `OR`,
`title:` and `*` wildcards; anything else is escaped rather than rejected.
Domain shorthand expands (CHARM, FF, EM, PID…). Regular-expression mode for
patterns like `FIC-\d{3,4}`. Per-book hit counts as a facet.

**Reader.** Several pages open at once — Ctrl+click or middle-click anything in
the left pane to open it beside what you are reading, + or Ctrl+T for a fresh
tab, Ctrl+Tab to cycle, and a tab menu for duplicate/close-others. Back/forward
per tab, dark/light/sepia, text scaling, find-on-page, the
merged keyword index of every book in one alphabet, favourites and history.
Pages are served over a registered `superdocs://` scheme, so nothing is ever
extracted to disk.

**Export.** PDF with a bookmark per topic and real selectable text; PNG; and a
`.sdoc` share pack — chosen pages with images embedded plus a generated index,
which opens in any browser with nothing installed.

**MCP server.** `SuperDocs serve` exposes the library read-only over stdio:
`docs_search`, `docs_read`, `docs_contents`, `docs_index`, `docs_books`,
`docs_stats`. Intended for nodes with no internet egress, where the vendor
documentation is already present and nothing can search it.

**WinHelp too.** `shared/winhelp` reads the format that came *before* .chm —
the one Windows itself can no longer open, because the viewer was dropped at
Vista and never replaced on 64-bit. Container, LZ77, both phrase-dictionary
formats, the topic stream and the keyword index, all clean-room. On the
ProVOX/ENVOX set that is **5,631 topics, 363,961 words, 12,702 index entries
over 7,093 terms and 5,694 cross-topic links** recovered from 14
otherwise-unopenable files — topic counts agreeing exactly with each file's
independently written title tree, every keyword reference and every link
resolving to a real topic, and **99.8% of titles decoding byte-identically,
eleven of the fourteen books at exactly 100%**.

**Its own look.** SuperDocs installs an aubergine-and-orchid palette through
`theme.use_palette()` instead of wearing the suite navy, so it is recognisable
among a dozen suite tools, and opens **light** by default — it is a tool for
reading long documents.

### Known gaps

- WinHelp character runs (which words were bold, or the hotspot) are not
  reproduced: the formatting stream decodes, but its alignment with the text
  does not, so a topic's links are listed at its foot instead of placed inline.
  Six `.hlp` titles out of 3,489 still decode imperfectly, visibly rather than
  silently.
- Highlight capture is not wired to the window (the store supports it).
- The version-diff view is not built, though the duplicate detection it needs is.
